doc.title: Billie Pierce and De De Pierce Interview, 1959-04-02

title: Favorite blues singers: Bessie Smith and Ma Rainey
summary: Billie says Bessie Smith was her favorite, disliked Ida Cox and Sara Martin, and compares Ma Rainey's heavy voice, recalling first playing for Bessie.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Bessie, Mamie, Ma Rainey: the classic blues queens

blocks.x: Well, there's one thing I forgot to ask Billy about your singing. Who were some of the best blues singers or other, any kind of singers that you heard when you were younger, coming up? That you, in other words, did you listen to any singers that you liked and maybe learnt from them? Something you could take lessons? Yeah, one for one. Who's that?
That's right, Bessie. That's her favorite.
Bessie Smith. Well, I liked all the rest of them, but Bessie Smith was just most wise. Bessie Smith, I didn't think too much of Ida Cox singing, I worked with Ida. I never didn't like her singing.
I never cared too much for her singing.

I never liked Ida singing. I didn't like Sarah Martin singing. I didn't like nobody but Bessie. Bessie, yeah. I liked Mama Rene, because Mama Rene was like, oh, you know, she was a ghetto. She was alright, I liked the way she started singing the blues. Bessie and Mama Rene were the two best blues songs I really cared anything for, because we really sang blues.
I heard Bessie several times in New York, but I never did hear Ma Rene. You heard Ma Rene?
How did she compare with her, Bessie? You say you liked Bessie best.
Yeah, I liked Bessie the best.
But how was Ma Rene? Have a deeper voice or how was...
Yeah, Mama, she had a deep voice. She had a heavy, gross voice.
She is powerful, as loud as...

Yeah, but down there she just didn't have enough of pep in her, you know. Not as much pep in her. Pep, you see, when you're first singing or something, you got to sing with a feeling or something, you know. If you make the house shake, well you're doing something. I know, I started doing that in New York. You know what I'm saying? And you see, when I worked with Bessie, I tell you the first song, Bessie, I don't say the first song, but the first song I played with her was, Walt Tilly, Won't You Take Your Time. You see, Tilly Brown was a dancing fool, she spent her night on the ballroom floor, I forgot it now, but I'm used to remember. And Bessie goes, Walt Tilly, Take Your Time. Oh, I was crazy about that, she was getting behind me all the time, I'm going to Belmont Theater, that's why she worked at Belmont Theater in Pensacola, Florida. Yeah, indeed. Bessie was my regular, Bessie Smith was my regular blues song, she was.
